newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels move into central Kisangani, soldiers loot.
newsitem.headline: Rebels move into central Kisangani, soldiers loot.

text.p: Rebels moved into Zaire's strategic third city of Kisangani on Saturday after overrunning its international airport where soldiers switched sides or just revolted and turned on Serb mercenary allies, diplomats said.
One Kisangani resident, contacted from the capital Kinshasa, said small groups of rebels had gathered in the city centre and that members of the population were coming out to welcome them.
Earlier, soldiers of Zaire's notoriously undisciplined army went on a looting spree in the city and then fled across the Zaire River, diplomats and aid workers said.
"What happened looks distinctly like a betrayal," a senior government official told Reuters, commenting on fighting between mercenaries and soldiers at the main airport.
A spokesman at rebel headquarters in the eastern town of Goma said rebel forces had advanced into Kisangani, nerve centre for Zaire's army operations in the war zone in the east.
"The international airport has been taken and fighting is continuing in town," Raphael Ngenda said.
But there was no independent confirmation of how much resistance, if any, they had met.
Some sources reported frightened civilians trying to flee across the river.

The fall of Kisangani would be the biggest setback for the government since the rebels took up arms in October, vowing to topple absent and ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko. They hold up to a fifth of the sprawling nation.

Kinshasa, traditional hotbed of opposition to Mobutu, remained calm but Friday night's events proved a shock for some. "I don't know what to think," a senior government official said. "We don't know whether the troops will obey their commanders."
A defence ministry official denied soldiers switched sides.
Senior government ministers were meeting in Kinshasa to evaluate the situation, he said.

France sent in a plane with an escort of 30 paratroops from its base in neighbouring Central African Republic and successfully airlifted out 15 foreign nationals. Aid sources said they used a second smaller airport, almost in town.

But Prime Minister Alain Juppe ruled out any unlateral military intervention by France, which has been lobbying unsuccessfully for a multi-national force to be sent to help aid get to refugees. Critics say its aim is to prop up Mobutu.
"We do not intend to launch again a solely French operation, and, after all, we do not have all the means to carry it out either," Juppe told a French television network.
Some diplomats said the much-heralded battle for Kisangani, a major port on the Zaire River, began after soldiers switched sides and clashed with mercenaries at the airport.
"There were clashes on the road from the airport when the mercenaries were trying to flee," one senior diplomat said. It was unclear how many of the 300 mercenaries escaped.
"The mercenaries fled the airport but nobody knows where they have gone. Some of the senior military seem to have gone across the river," a senior Western diplomat said.
The rebels accuse Zaire of denying them citizenship and preparing to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.
Zaire accuses neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of invading in support of the rebels. All three deny the charge.
The government has accepted a U.N. ceasefire plan. The rebels have resisted diplomatic pressure for a ceasefire.
Mobutu has been out of the country for most of the time since August when he had prostate cancer surgery in Europe.
